Goldman Sachs Interview
Experience
Ishaan Chandak
TY IT
INTRODUCTION
Hello, I'm Ishaan Chadnak, and I belong to the field of Information Technology. I would
like to share my interview journey for the Summer Internship position at Goldman
Sachs.

ONLINE ASSESSMENT
Date : 08/08/2023
Time: 8:00 AM (Duration →1 hour)
Platform: HackerRank
The online assessment consisted of 10 multiple-choice questions (MCQs), 2 coding
questions, and 2 HR-related questions. We were allocated 50 minutes to complete the
MCQs and coding questions, and an additional 10 minutes for the HR questions. For each
correct MCQ answer, we earned +5 marks, while an incorrect answer resulted in a
deduction of -2 marks. These are the questions I can recall from the assessment.
MCQ’s:
1. We were presented with a mathematical expression and asked to determine the
maximum stack size required when converting it from 'infix' to 'postfix' notation.
2. We were tasked with calculating the percentage reduction in the number of bits
when applying "Huffman Coding" to encode a set of letters, along with their
respective frequencies.
3.
There was a coding problem involving multi-level inheritance and method
overriding. We had to predict the output when invoking a member function from
a derived class.
4. In a probability and combinatorics (PnC) question, we were asked to find the
count of 5-digit numbers greater than or equal to 50,000 that contained the digits 6
and 9, with the condition that 9 must appear before 6, and all digits should be
distinct.
5. We encountered a Resource Allocation Graph related to Operating Systems and
CPU Scheduling, involving Request Edges and Resource Edges. The task was to
determine the optimal process execution sequence to avoid deadlocks.
6. There was a question related to AVL Trees, although the exact details are not
remembered.
7. We were given either the preorder or postorder traversal of a binary search tree
and had to reconstruct the tree.
8. There was also a coding problem for which we needed to predict the output.
1

Coding Questions:
There were two questions in total. Out of which I was able to solve one because I had no
time for the other one
First Question :
A binary tree is given. We had to find the sum MagicSum of the tree. MagicSum is the
sum of all Magic Nodes. Magic Node is the one whose one child is a factor of the other. In
this we weren’t given the tree in the form of Nodes and its left or right child pointing to
other nodes.
In the question,
The tree was represented as a series of relationships of each node to the Root node such
as L, R, LL, LR.. and so on, where each node is left (L) to Root or left-left (LL) or right-left
(RL) to Root and so on
Input Format:
The first line of input contains an integer, N number of nodes in the tree The second line
of input contains an Integer root which is the root of the tree.The next N-1 lines of input
contain a string, S, and an integer, X separated by a single white space where X is a node
in the tree and S is the relation between Root and X.
Sample Input:
9
11
L 23
R 44
LL 13
LR 9
RL 22
RR 7
RLL 6
RLR 15
2

Can you recall a specific project where you invested significant effort, and what was your
emotional response upon successfully completing it?
Out of the 10 MCQs I submitted only 8 and I had guessed one of them. Also, I was only
able to solve 1 coding question with all the test cases passing.
ONLINE ASSESSMENT RESULTS
On the 23rd of August, around 6:00 pm, the shortlist was announced. Coincidentally, this
was the same day when Chandrayaan-3 was making its moon landing. I was in the
company of my friends and my mom as we all gathered to witness this historic event.
Just as we were engrossed in the lunar landing, my phone suddenly rang. It was my
friend calling to offer congratulations because I had been selected as one of the 12
students shortlisted for the interviews. I was taken aback, so I quickly checked my email
to confirm the news, and upon seeing the results, I was overwhelmed with joy.
The interviews were scheduled for the 25th of August, which meant I had just two days to
prepare. This understandably made me quite anxious. Without wasting any time, I
reached out to my senior peers for advice on how to proceed. Their guidance was to go
through past interview experiences (much like the one you're reading 😉) and also
review all the fundamental concepts in computer science.
INTERVIEW ROUND 1
Date : 25/08/2023
Time: 9:00 AM (Duration →1 hour)
Platform: Zoom and HackerRank CodePair
The link to the Zoom meeting where the interviews would take place was provided to us.
All of us were told to go to Zoom's breakout space. The first four students were
interviewed in a matter of minutes. The rest of them remained in the breakout space.
After about 30 minutes, a pop informed me that I was being transferred to a different
room for my initial interview. A meeting coordinator (of GS) was in charge of overseeing
all tasks associated with zoom, such as sending participants to breakout rooms or
7

interviewers meeting rooms.
The interview began, and the interviewer greeted me warmly and in a laid-back manner.
Then she asked me to give my introduction. To impress the interviewer, I advise creating
a very strong and impactful introduction. She then instructed me to open the Hackerrank
codepair interface that had been given to us prior to the interviews (this does not mean
you need to brag). Every single one of us had a unique codepair link. The Hacker Rank
Codepair interface looks like,
Surprisingly the first question she asked was quite simple, she wanted me to basically
concat two strings without changing the first two strings and then print the answer. I
gave her all the solutions that I could think of at the moment. The answer is available at
this link. Then she asked me to code any one but the only condition she mentioned was
not to use .concat() function. This was very basic and an easy question.
After this she moved to the second question. The Snakes and Ladders question. The
answer to this is available here. I wasn’t asked to code this but explain my thinking. The
ans that I gave involved using a queue of pairs of pair<int, int> where I will store the
index and the number of steps required to reach that index. The interviewer actually
made me do an entire dry run for the first 6 steps and then I guess was content with my
answer.
After answering that, she proceeded to ask me, "If you have four different messages, how
many minimum bits will you need to transmit that message?" I stated at the outset that
Huffman coding can be used to tackle this problem in the best way possible. I then
8

asserted that this problem can be solved with just 2 bits if the message frequency is
ignored. This is so that we can identify the messaged utilising the 2 bit's 4 possible
permutations. Additionally, I expanded a little on the huffman coding section because I
think it's crucial to essentially giving the interviewer more information than they asked
for. They are somewhat impressed by this.
She questioned me about segmentation errors at the conclusion of the conversation. I
responded, and the last question was whether I had any other questions. I didn't ask any
questions during this round, and I was then instructed to leave and return to the
breakout area to wait for the next round of interviews.
INTERVIEW ROUND 2
Date : 25/08/2023
Time: 12:00 pm (Duration →40mins)
Platform: Zoom
This round came as a complete surprise; it felt more like an in-depth discussion with the
interviewer. Initially, the interview followed the usual pattern, starting with the request
for my self-introduction, to which I provided the prepared introduction I had. Then came
a barrage of questions. The interviewer began by asking about my preferred
programming language, to which I mentioned C++. He then delved into whether I had
worked on any projects using C++. While I hadn't worked on C++ projects specifically, I
explained that I used it extensively for Data Structures and Algorithms. Unexpectedly, the
interviewer veered into a topic, Garbage Collector, typically associated with Java. I hadn't
listed Java as a skill on my resume or during the interview, so I was momentarily taken
aback. However, I recalled reading about it recently during my Object-Oriented
Programming studies. I answered to the best of my knowledge, even adding a connection
to C++ (Destructors) to my response. It seemed like my answer satisfied the interviewer.
Next, he inquired about my familiarity with Database Management Systems (DBMS). I
expressed my confidence in DBMS, prompting him to ask me to describe the types of
DBMS. I went into detail about various types, such as relational and network-based
databases, even though he was primarily interested in SQL and NoSQL databases.
Subsequently, he asked if I had any knowledge of key-value databases, and I explained
the concept, emphasizing the unique key for identifying values.
He then inquired about document-based databases, and although I couldn't provide a
9

perfect definition, my reference to MongoDB seemed to assure him of my understanding.
The interview took an unexpected turn when he asked if I had heard of Columnar
databases. With no prior knowledge of this concept, I sought clarification and requested
examples or a rough idea to provide a meaningful response. His explanation revealed
that he was merely assessing my familiarity with the term, not posing a serious question,
which brought a sense of relief.
Then, the conversation shifted to the topic of multithreading, an area we had extensively
discussed. He initiated by asking about the fundamentals of threads, the distinctions
between threads and processes, and the advantages of threads in concurrent
programming. As our discussion progressed, he posed a more intricate question about
how threads create the illusion of multiprocessing. My initial response didn't seem to
meet his expectations, so I politely inquired about the answer he had in mind, to which
he suggested revisiting the question later in the interview.
Subsequently, he presented a scenario: a 100GB file with all white spaces replaced by "%"
signs and asked for the most optimal approach to rectify this using a 4-core system.
Initially, I proposed a somewhat brute-force solution as my immediate thought process
was limited. However, I then suggested dividing the file into manageable blocks and
processing them concurrently on the four cores, which he found somewhat better but
not ideal. Finally, I proposed utilizing an Inplace Merge Sort approach to further divide
the file into smaller packets, thereby enhancing processing speed and efficiency. This
approach seemed to satisfy him, although he inquired if I had any other ideas.
Regrettably, I had exhausted all my mental resources in devising this solution. This part
of the interview concluded on that note.
The conversation shifted towards cloud computing, and he inquired about my
knowledge in this area. I mentioned my familiarity with SaaS (Software as a Service) and
cited my experience using Google's Compute Engine, a virtual machine, in one of my
projects. He followed up by asking if cloud computing was restricted solely to software,
to which I responded in the negative. I elaborated on the utilization of GPUs and TPUs
available on platforms like Google Colab and Kaggle Notebooks. My response appeared to
satisfy him, and he expressed his contentment with my answer.
Towards the end of the interview, the interviewer invited me to ask any questions I
might have. I took the opportunity to revisit the multithreading question, which he felt I
hadn't fully addressed. He then elaborated on topics related to the "fork()" function and
similar concepts. Interestingly, I had mentioned this during my initial response, but it
10

seemed he hadn't recalled it at the time.
In a surprising turn of events, I recognized that my interviewer was the same person I
had seen during the Goldman Sachs presentation. I mentioned this observation at the
conclusion of the interview, leading to a discussion about the presentation and other
attendees who were present during the event. My interviewer expressed his admiration
for my attention to detail and remarkable memory, especially considering that the
presentation had occurred approximately 20 days earlier.
This marked the end of my second round and I was then sent to the breakout room.
During my time in the breakout room, I noticed that there were initially seven people
present. When I checked my email just after the second round, I discovered that the
company had sent a list of seven students who had been shortlisted for the second round.
After sometime everyone joined the breakout room after completing their second round.
Out of the seven shortlisted candidates, two were selected for the third round interviews,
but unfortunately, I wasn't among them. After they completed their interviews, the rest
of us remained, awaiting our turns to be called.
After a while, the meeting coordinator entered the Breakout Room and informed us that
the interview rounds had concluded, and we were free to exit the meeting. This occurred
at approximately 1:40 PM. Someone in the room inquired about the results' release, and
the coordinator mentioned that the results would be available by 4:00 PM.
RESULTS
I was quite tensed after the interviews. I came back home from my dad’s office, the place
I was giving my interview from. I was eating my lunch where I just checked my mail. I
jumped in happiness as I could see I was one of the 3 students selected for internships.
